0c15121c-bdb4-5d29-91aa-079d86d55f11.description2: In the latter half of the 19th century, many European countries held exhibitions about their colonies, both during world fairs and smaller events. France used world fairs to "showcase" their colonies, both in the great Paris world fairs as well as smaller, colonial fairs organised in Marseille (1906, 1922) and Paris (1931). These expositions glorified colonial expansion, particularly by offering visitors an "object lesson". Tunisia took the spotlight in 1906 due to the central role it played in the ongoing dispute with Italy. The "indigenous villages", such as the one pictured in this photograph, were above all representations of the way Europeans imagined their colonies. They were later described as "human zoos" by historians of the late 20th century, due to the horrific practice of putting people for display as if they were animals.

0fbf5343-64ee-545a-b2c8-56f70b18ca50.description2: Samovars are very common in Russia, Eastern Europe and in the Middle East. The samovar is a highly decorated metal container with a tap at the bottom and a pipe that runs vertically through it. By filling the pipe with coals, it will heat the water inside the container. A teapot kept on the top of the pipe will brew a strong concentration of tea that will be served after adding boiled water to it from the container. Samovars were brought to Jordan by various north Caucasian peoples, referred to as Circassians, who immigrated to the region during the last quarter of the 19th century.

159f7828-e467-5f3d-b3ba-96aafc6f5b7c.description:
This postcard (not franked or used) is part of a collection donated by the anthropologist Manuel Antón.  
During the second half of the nineteenth century in Europe and America there were held countless ethnological and colonial exhibitions that showed groups of individuals from distant exotic territories, to make them public and available to anthropologists and scholars. They were put on show alongside exotic animals and recreations of the structures inhabited by these people in their places of origin.  
These exhibitions were a result of the intensification of colonial imperialism of the West and also the relative popularity of two young scientific disciplines (physical anthropology and ethnology) and the development of new and intense forms of consumerism among the European bourgeoisie. Actually these exhibitions got to transmit a sense of lower and "savage" status of the colonised people (Sánchez Gómez, L. “Espectáculos demasiado humanos”, 2008, 88-89).

27f25605-a0d6-5226-be64-b5c88fc6fc1c.name: *Fall of Stalać*
27f25605-a0d6-5226-be64-b5c88fc6fc1c.author: Petar Petrovic
27f25605-a0d6-5226-be64-b5c88fc6fc1c.description2:
Having mastered the cobbling trade and after studying theology, in 1873, the Serb Đorđe Krstić went to further his education at the Munich Art Academy thanks to a scholarship from the Knez that came after he had prepared for admission to an arts and crafts school. By 1920, there were approximately 50 Serbian students enrolled there. Though pieces from his Munich phase measure up to the best works of the time, a later painting by this historical and genre artist is better suited here. After the initial, strong influence of realism, on his return to Belgrade, in 1883, he endeavoured to present an open manner of painting, with strong and coloristic effects.  
Stalać was one of the largest fortified towns in Serbia in the Middle Ages, serving simultaneously as a checkpoint on the approaches to the then capital Kruševac and to strategically important valleys. At the same time as four other forts, Stalać was burned down and laid to waste in 1413, in initial raids by the Ottoman Turks, who subsequently conquered Serbia in 1459.  
This painting was commissioned by King Aleksandar Obrenović for the 1900 Paris Exposition. However, the committee rejected it before the Expo for an excessively extreme depiction of fighting. When the painting was exhibited in the National Museum in Belgrade in 1901, 1,000 visitors flocked to see it every day.

2ae3984e-4d68-5007-ab52-077d0d39f896.description2: The Alhambra, the palace and fortress of the Moorish Kings of Granada, Spain, was founded in 1248 and largely completed by 1354. After three hundred years of neglect and destruction, restoration work began in 1828. Its sumptuous architecture excited a great deal of interest, dissemninated most notably by the *Plans, Details and Sections of the Alhambra* published by Owen Jones from 1836. Of the original furnishings of the Palace, some vases survive. The most famous was made before 1400 and is here copied relatively accurately by Deck. This vase was probably shown in the International Exhibition, London, 1862.

2c586151-177a-57bd-9616-76904bd42503.description2: The Italian Orientalist painter Stefano Ussi's painting *Surre Regiment* depicts the deva caravan carrying gifts from Cairo to Kaaba, the pilgrims and a regiment of the Ottoman army assigned to protect the caravan. *Surre Regiment* is the largest painting of the Painting Collection of the National Palaces. The composition reflects the emotions of Muslims during the pilgrimage to Mecca, whose ethnic structures, growing styles and points of view regarding Islam are different. The frame of the painting dated 1873 is surrounded by Arabic Kufic script, which is a part of the 126th verse in Surah Al-Imran that reads, “There is no help or victory except from Allah, the All-Mighty, the All-Wise”. *Surre Regiment* is presumed to be included in the Palace’s collection by being purchased or given by Mısır Hıdivi as a gift for Sultan Abdülaziz.

30b613c8-c840-5eba-a2ea-3334a058e6c5.name: *The Temptations of Saint Antony*
30b613c8-c840-5eba-a2ea-3334a058e6c5.author: Marina Minozzi
30b613c8-c840-5eba-a2ea-3334a058e6c5.keywords: Realism; France; La tentation de Saint-Antoine; Orientalism; Orientalist painting; religious topics; exoticism; eroticism; woman; international exhibitions; universal exposition; national exposition; exoticism in fine arts and literature

30b613c8-c840-5eba-a2ea-3334a058e6c5.description2:
The painting by Domenico Morelli shown at the Universal Exposition in Paris, it’s among the artist’s most complex artworks. Both realistic and symbolic elements characterise the painting, as well as a strong mystic, but at the same time erotic, tension. Inspired by *La Tentation de Saint-Antoine* by Gustave Flaubert from 1874, the painting shows realism in the imaginary setting influenced by oriental elements. The work was finished in 1878 and sent to the French merchant Goupil to be shown at the Universal Exposition in Paris. It was also presented at the National Exposition in Turin in 1880 and completely misunderstood by contemporaries who blamed Morelli for having resigned to make fashionable art.  
A smaller version of it was painted by the artist while making a lot of preparatory drawings in which Saint Anthony is standing next to the rock wall. In the final version the Saint is seated on the ground trying to resist the temptations embodied by the two half-naked women on the left.

3540af77-ea01-5e4b-bd04-3e31d3b139e4.description2: Leopoldo Metlicovitz worked as a lithographer and an illustrator. Among his works are illustrations for the Milanese newspaper *La Sera*, opera librettos and some cover pages of *Corriere della Sera*. He also made posters for an auto exhibition, an insurance company and the opening of the Simplon Tunnel in 1906. The erotic male nude recalls Michelangelo’s figures. The poster was chosen by the Committee of the International Exhibition despite the fact the it was not submitted within the competition. The artist depicts the personification of Progress and Science ideally leading the convoy towards the light beyond the tunnel. The tunnel, almost 20 kilometres long, was started following an 1895 agreement between Italy and Switzerland. The works were finished after long difficulties and the railway was opened on June 1, 1906 and celebrated at the Universal Exposition in Milan.

35645306-e708-561a-ae81-24e697df6d15.author: Petar Petrovic
35645306-e708-561a-ae81-24e697df6d15.description2: In order to evoke and convey the spirit of the Balkans and the Orient as faithfully as possible, Paja Jovanović meticulously recorded each detail of the interior of a typical Balkan or Eastern house. He also collected props that made up a family’s inventory of furniture (e.g. the hexagonal decorative table to the left), and carefully studied the physiognomies and characters of the men and women he encountered in the southern Balkans, in Egypt, Constantinople, the Caucasus and elsewhere. The precision of draughtsmanship and freshness of colour in this painting by Paja Jovanović ranks it among his more successful works from the mid-1880s.

36d58a55-2db8-5fb1-a95f-93e3fa5513d2.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul; Pascal Sebah
36d58a55-2db8-5fb1-a95f-93e3fa5513d2.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.description2: Giuseppe Parvis, who emigrated from Italy to Egypt, began extensive production of elegant furniture adapted to Arabian taste and decorated with mother-of-pearl and metal inserts. He won awards for his work at the Universal Exhibitions of Paris in 1867, Vienna and Philadelphia. Giuseppe Parvis is an example of successful businessman who successfully adapted to the Egyptian market. He was able to run laboratories with 50 workers and trained a large number of students in ebony furniture making. Over the span of 20 years he introduced and sold furniture to Arabian people who traditionally did not possess such furniture, using an Arabic style and taste and by using woods found in the East, Egypt and China.

386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.author: Marina Minozzi

386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.third_name: *Edoardo Jenner inocula il vaccino del vaiolo al figlio*
386fe084-5d31-5abb-9f36-fb457dd43935.description2: Giulio Monteverde was an Italian sculptor who started carving wooden crucifixes before moving on to sculpture during his years at the Academy of Fine Arts in Genoa. In 1865 Monteverde moved to Rome to study at the Academy of St. Luke. The sculpture of Edward Jenner (1749-1823) represents the British physician and naturalist inoculating for the first time, on his own son, the smallpox vaccine that he invented. This work was initially rejected by the Academy of St. Luke, entrusted with selecting works of art for the International Exposition in Vienna, but then exhibited in it thanks to an influential friend. The plaster cast of Jenner won the gold medal in Vienna, and a similar success was had with the marble version presented at the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878 when it won the medal of honor. The bronze version shown in the picture represents Jenner administering the smallpox vaccine to his son, blending dynamism and details in the face of the scientist, clothes and objects.

All of them are cited in the Chronological List of 1853, which includes 12 studies depicting exotic animals done in The Jardin des Plantes in Paris. The series is considered the preparatory base for the amazing painting *Dopo il Diluvio. Uscita degli animali dall’Arca* (*After the Flood. The Animals Exiting the Ark*), commissioned by King Vittorio Emanuele II for the Museum of Capodimonte and presented in 1867 at the Universal Exposition in Paris. Other animals, like the Indian ox, the antelope and the dromedary were depicted in the Jardin des Plantes in Paris with the same aim.

3cce65e9-b5bd-5b53-9b90-2b8d522d809b.description2: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The motif of glass filaments worked with pincers to look like crests, typical of the 17th century objects is used also in the ruby-red glass cup with snake-shaped stem of neo-baroque inspiration and dating from the second half of the 19th century. Its form is inspired by snake goblets common in Venice and Germany in the 17th century.

3d0e79a0-084c-5267-9ebf-6210134cee94.author: Marina Minozzi
3d0e79a0-084c-5267-9ebf-6210134cee94.third_name: Galleria Nazionale di Arte Moderna, Roma
3d0e79a0-084c-5267-9ebf-6210134cee94.description2: The Pavilion of Fine Arts, built for the 1911 International Exhibition in Rome and meant to become the permanent location of the National Gallery of Modern Art, was designed by the architect Cesare Bazzani (1873-1939). He also was responsible for the Department of Public Education and the layout of the Tiberine island. The Pavilion covered an area of 5000 square meters and was constructed in only 15 months. The building was designed in a sober classic style that merged perfectly with the environment and city landscape. The massive facade with the huge staircase and twin columns drew inspiration from ancient Roman architecture; the architect added to it more recent elements like Seicento festoons and the Borghese coat of arms with the eagle. The building celebrated the 50th anniversary from the Risorgimento (the unification of Italy) and affirmed the authority of the Italian state among the other countries.

401e4018-e1ee-5a6d-87f6-467eb15b5da9.description2: In 1911 the city of Turin organized an International Exhibition in the Valentino park, on the banks of the Po River. Beyond the Isabella Bridge another huge park was built to house entertainment and attractions. One of the most popular attractions was the so-called "Kermesse Orientale", in which the public experienced the illusion of making a journey through the different parts of the Eastern world. Five new areas were built, according to photographs taken at the time. The first one represented Arabian, Egyptian, Tunisian and Turkish environments while the fourth area reproduced Japan and India. The park also showcased a harem, a mosque and a Moorish school and the visitors could enjoy belly dancing shows and walks on camelback.

He arranged 72 examples of warriors coming from almost every part of the world in a three-room exhibit. These characters were modelled from actual examples and resembled Arabic, Australian, African and Indian people with costumes and features. The exhibition paid great attention to facial renderings and the physical appearance of the warriors.

412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.description2: “The Chronicle of the Universal Exhibition of Paris” of 1878 celebrates the city of Murano’s commercial success in glass production. A large number of these objects reside in the collection of the Museum of Industrial Arts in Rome (M.A.I.), now part of the acquisitions of the National Museum of Antique Art on display at Palazzo Barberini. M.A.I. was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. These jars were manufactured by the famous glass company Salviati, founded in 1866 and established in Venice and Murano. In presenting these objects they claimed the rebirth of a long-forgotten antique art and the rebirth of glass industries in Italy. Tomb excavations brought to light a series of vases. New objects based on those excavated were made on the occasion of the International Exhibition in Paris in 1878.

459c2899-4ce2-5ffd-a17b-a43ffa91c9bc.name: *Milos Obrenovic, prince of Serbia*
459c2899-4ce2-5ffd-a17b-a43ffa91c9bc.author: Petar Petrovic
459c2899-4ce2-5ffd-a17b-a43ffa91c9bc.description2: Milos Obrenović (1783-1860) was Prince of Serbia from 1815 to 1839, and again from 1858 to 1860. He participated in the First Serbian Uprising, led Serbs in the Second Serbian Uprising, and founded the dynasty of Obrenović. Under his rule, Serbia became an autonomous duchy within the Ottoman Empire. He is credited with starting the process of re-establishing Serbian statehood, as well as shaping the domestic and foreign policies of the modern Serbian state. Prince Milos ruled autocratically, permanently refusing to share power. During his rule, he was the richest man in Serbia and among the richest in the Balkans. In the portrait that was painted by Pavel Djurkovitch in Kragujevac, prince Milos is dressed in Oriental costume and has on the top of the head a turban. It is a typically Oriental piece of costume and this was of significance for the attitude and dignity of the Serbian sovereign at the beginning 19th century, who was by all means respecting an Ottoman empire and his Sultan.

48a64aba-b279-5473-911b-51ced2c8a938.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

4b63a853-7b5d-5c93-8ec7-7348d5091101.name: Model in plaster
4b63a853-7b5d-5c93-8ec7-7348d5091101.description: Following on the European fascination for the oriental world and for the famous Nasrid Palace of the Alhambra (Granada), a lot of reproductions of its remarkable architecture and decorations were made and spread. José Contreras was commended as restorer and decorator and his son, Rafael (1824–1890), was the leading pioneer of this trend in 1847. His work was continued by the grandson and by a huge number of plaster-cast workshops in Granada, and very likely, in other cities. His plasterworks were very successful in the International Exhibitions and were kept in private collections and museums like South Kensington (London). These delightful polychrome models, accentuated with a black frame, represents different rooms form the Alhambra Palace as the Comares Room, with its double horseshoe.

4bc8852b-4eb9-5ea3-a533-cfbbadd4a2f8.name: *Coronation Of Tsar Dušan*
4bc8852b-4eb9-5ea3-a533-cfbbadd4a2f8.author: Petar Petrovic
4bc8852b-4eb9-5ea3-a533-cfbbadd4a2f8.description2: *The Coronation of Tsar Dušan* was painted on commission from the Kingdom of Serbia for the 1900 Paris Exposition. Jovanović began to prepare for it two years ahead, taking trips and gathering material in Vienna (Habsburg Court Library), Constantinople, Venice, Skopje, Kosovo and Metohija (Gračanica Monastery). Jovanović's consultant in the creation of this piece was the renowned Serbian historian Stojan Novaković. The artist used the *plein air* (outdoor) painting technique fashionable at the time, one of the reasons being the wish of the commissioning party, more specifically King Milan Obrenović, that Jovanović produce a work suitable for crafting a large tapestry. The painting was unveiled at the 1900 Paris Exposition, drawing flattering recognition and praise and winning a gold medal. The artist was somewhat unhappy with the choice of painting technique, and repeated the subject of Tsar Dušan's coronation (or the Proclamation of Dušan's Code, as it was called for a time after World War II) on numerous occasions after the Paris Expo, in various formats, in different ways and for various purposes until late in life. The fact that there are more than ten replicas and variants by the author himself known to date, speaks of how much this work was esteemed and sought after.

4dcb750e-6c2b-5848-924b-43fb6905059d.name: Memorial Volume – Dedicatory and opening ceremonies of the Chicago World's Colombian Exposition – 1893
4dcb750e-6c2b-5848-924b-43fb6905059d.description2: The World's Columbian Exposition or The Chicago World's Fair was a World's Fair held in Chicago in 1893 to celebrate the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus' arrival in the New World in 1492. The fair was an influential social and cultural event to which the Ottoman Empire had been invited. It displayed raw materials and agricultural products at the exposition, as well as handicraft products and plant products belonging to the palace revenue. The 1893 Chicago Exhibition was a big success for the Chamber of Commerce. The Head of the Chamber of Commerce, Azaryan Efendi, was assigned to the head of the commission, which was formed in Istanbul for the Chicago Exhibition.

4e04768a-5d14-5f0c-94df-814f2d4400f7.name: *The Exhibition!! The triumph of industry*
4e04768a-5d14-5f0c-94df-814f2d4400f7.description2: Alfred Rodiba (1848–1926) was the artist of many dystopian works, a very fashionable theme at the time. Although he appreciated the 1889 Exposition Universelle (world fair), the cartoonist inside him also noticed a "universal" worship of industry which made everyone unaware of the pollution these inventions were producing.

4f6d8c3a-63e3-50c0-b243-faaa3ddd2001.name: *The Expulsion of the Duke of Athens*
4f6d8c3a-63e3-50c0-b243-faaa3ddd2001.author: Marina Minozzi
4f6d8c3a-63e3-50c0-b243-faaa3ddd2001.keywords: Painting; Italian painters; history painting; celebration of the past; international exhibition; universal exposition; art exhibition; Esposizione nazionale; Florence; post-unitaria Italian society; national identity

4f6d8c3a-63e3-50c0-b243-faaa3ddd2001.description2: The painting is a second version by the artist of his masterpiece *La cacciata del Duca di Atene* started by Ussi in 1854 in Rome and finished in Florence, now at the National Gallery of Modern Art in Florence. The artwork was presented at the National Exhibition in Florence in 1861 and sent at the International Exhibition in Paris in 1867 where it was awarded the silver medal. The scene depicted in the painting refers to the book *Istorie Fiorentine* by Nicolò Machiavelli. In particular the painter shows the moment in which Gualtieri di Brienne, Duke of Athens between 1342-43, abdicates from Florence. To his left are the republicans who force him to sign. The second version is slightly different from the original one in characters and manner. The painting shows the city of Florence, represented by the republicans, defending its freedom from a cruel ruler and embodies a strong political, civic and moral relevance, emphasised by the sheer size of the canvas.

6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.name: Moroccan House in Linderhof  Palace Park
6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.type: Pavillion; Park building in Linderhof Palace Park
6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.history:
When the rebuilding of the “Moorish Kiosk” in the Linderhof park undertaken by order of Ludwig II was completed at the beginning of 1878, it evidently reawakened the king’s interest in buildings in the Islamic architectural style.  
The pavilion, acquired at the World Exhibition in Paris in 1878, was remodelled inside at Ludwig II's request and originally built on the Stockalpe near the Austrian border. The "Moroccan House" had already also been shown at the International Exhibition in Vienna in 1873 and had been built for this purpose in Morocco. The wooden building, acquired by a private individual after the king's death, was bought back by the state in 1980 and was reconstructed in the palace park in 1998.
6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.keywords: King Ludwig II; Linderhof Palace; Ettal; Moorish style; Romanticism; gardens
6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.description2: The king had considerable alterations made to both the outside and the inside of the house in keeping with his own lavish tastes. Jean Perron, a sculptor in Paris who had organised the purchase for Ludwig II, also acquired the rich furnishings appropriate for an ornamental setting such as tables, chandeliers, tabourets, mirrors and vessels, none of which have been preserved. Numerous skilled workers and artists were involved in the dismantling, rebuilding and altering of the house.The entire colour scheme was changed with an abundant use of gold, and individual rooms were furnished with costly materials. Coloured glazing “in the Moorish style” and a tessellated floor were introduced to add to the oriental character of the house.

637e27e9-204e-5721-869e-ad4380dc0140.name: *The great celestial globe. 1900 Exposition Universelle.*
637e27e9-204e-5721-869e-ad4380dc0140.description2: A great celestial globe, measuring 50 metres in diameter and located near the Champ de Mars, was one of the proposed attractions for the 1900 Paris World Fair. A restaurant sat beneath it, and popular science activities inside the globe allowed the visitors to learn about astronomy. Other than the globe's colossal dimensions, the poster also foresees great crowds of people visiting the exhibit.

6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.keywords: Sculpture; Italian sculptors; realism; Verismo; social topics; post-unitarian Italian society; rights of workers; working class; life expectancy; poverty; industry; communication; industrial development; road; railway; international; universal exposition
6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
6c348586-1356-5ba4-b2b5-0c09d19282dc.description2: Vincenzo Vela studied at the academy of Fine arts of Brera and at the age of 22 he won an Academy of Venice competition. The artwork is an homage to the workers who died during the construction of the Gotthard Tunnel between 1872-82, which had implemented new cost-lowering techniques that also caused numerous incidents and loss of life. Work conditions were very unhealthy: temperatures over 30 degrees, gas exhalations and no air shafts. Even the accommodations were unhealthy and dirty. When the workers went on strike for the inhumane conditions, police shot at protesters, killing four workers. The miners in *The Victims of Labour* are depicted carrying the body of a dying classmate on a stretcher out of the tunnel. A self-portrait of the sculptor is recognisable in the classmate’s face. The harsh modelling of the workers’ bodies, almost deformed, makes the scene even more powerful. The artist affirmed he had no commission for this work which was a passion project. In 1895 it was cast in bronze on request of the Ministry of Education; in 1900 it was sent to the Universal Exhibition in Paris.

6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.description2:
Cesare Trionfo was a child when he migrated with his family to Tunisia from Livorno in 1855. He became a trader, and in 1886 he started trading musical instruments. In Tunis, he later also started a shop that made musical instruments such as this organ. Trionfo promoted the construction of the theatre Politeama Roissini, which he co-owned.  
This organ was exhibited in Milan for the 1906 international exhibition. The organ is a traditional Italian musical instrument. This one has decorative elements taken from Arab architecture.

750a06a9-2d0d-5ed4-96b6-1e5b28d3634e.name: Plan of the park Bibescu
750a06a9-2d0d-5ed4-96b6-1e5b28d3634e.description2: In 1898, Nicolae Romanescu, the mayor of Craiova (a city in Wallachia), hired French landscape architect Edouard Redont to lay out two parks in Craiova. One of them, called park Bibescu, was completed in 1903. It was built on a terrain bought by the city hall of Craiova in 1853 from Iancu Bibescu, brother of Wallachian prince Gheorghe Bibescu. The park occupied a surface of 100 ha, among which 4 were represented by water. Some of the attractions of the park included: a luxuriant vegetation, two lakes, a waterfall river, several springs, a replica of a medieval castle, a suspended bridge, a zoo. There also existed restaurants and cafes, a library, an exhibition hall, a ceremony hall, a hippodrome, a velodrome and a pier. In 1900 the plan of park Bibescu was awarded a gold medal at the universal exposition of Paris.

This show was meant to celebrate ethnography as a new science and, at the same time, to highlight the habits and customs of the different regions of Italy, especially on the occasion of the 50th anniversary celebrations of the unification of the Italian state. A consequence of the exhibition was an enlargement of the city of Rom and massive urban growth. At the same time, upon the Rassegna Illustrata dell’Esposizione commercial pavilions were destined to later become restaurants, shops and pubs. All of them were clearly inspired by the popularity of orientalism.

77e11861-c38b-50a8-8fb9-b72467f69e2b.description2: At the International Exhibition in Paris, 1878, the Algerian Pavilion was designed by the architect M. Wable, who was appointed by General Chanzy. The building represents one of the greatest proofs of French colonisation policy. The front-door, four metres wide, is a copy from the ‘Ubbad Mosque of Sidi Bumadyan in Tlemcen, and is richly decorated with enamelled majolica and arabesque decorations. The decorations of the minaret echo the tower in ruins from the mosque of Mansoura, 1,200 square metres wide. The pavilion was meant to show the productive potential of the colony to the French capitalists.

77f7d1f5-f298-526e-8bfa-21c5a75d09f2.name: *4 June 1913, Gand, \[pavillion from\] the French Protectorate in Morocco \[Exposition Universelle et Internationale\]*
77f7d1f5-f298-526e-8bfa-21c5a75d09f2.description2: In 1913, Gand (Belgium) hosted the 28th Exposition Universelle (world fair). Like France, Belgium gave pride of place to its colonies. During its universal expositions (world fairs), France tended to exhibit a number of colonial pavilions, whose architecture and "exoticism" fascinated visitors. The "Pavilion from the French Protectorate in Morocco" was built to show off the recent (1912) Moroccan protectorate.

7a9b5caa-c0ca-5b9c-a54b-4f65a9d0be8e.name: *Palais de l'Industrie. July to November 1890. International Exhibition of the Industrial Arts and Sciences*
7a9b5caa-c0ca-5b9c-a54b-4f65a9d0be8e.second_name: *Concerts every day, directed by Mayeur of the Opera*
7a9b5caa-c0ca-5b9c-a54b-4f65a9d0be8e.description2: The Palais de l'Industrie et des Beaux-Arts was built in Paris in 1855 with the purpose of hosting the first French Exposition Universelle (world fair). Its great glass and metal structure, the "galerie des machines", was a symbol of industrial progress. This building, unlike others of its kind, was used for the same purpose right up until 1896, when it was destroyed to make space for the Grand Palais and the Petit Palais for the Exposition Universelle of 1900. For 40 years it hosted a variety of exhibits, all aimed at promoting recent technological innovations.

7d67ccb5-cf82-5111-bc4d-df565effb29b.name: *Guernsey and Jersey, Malta and Ceylon* (from *Dickinson's Comprehensive Pictures of the Great Exhibition*)
7d67ccb5-cf82-5111-bc4d-df565effb29b.description:
The Great Exhibition of London, held at the Crystal Palace in 1851, was a notable event for the world for various reasons: It was the very first exhibition of this kind, and it was possible, for the first time, to gather and wonder at products from distant countries at the Crystal Palace, a futuristic building for the time and a symbol of the cosmopolitan nature of the United Kingdom.  
  
*Dickinson’s Comprehensive Pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851* (published in 1854) is a famous collection of coloured illustrations of the Great Exhibition. The illustration displayed on this page, painted by Joseph Nash, shows the stands with the products of Ceylon and Malta, as well as those of British Channel Islands Guernsey and Jersey, and gives an accurate depiction of what the interior of the Crystal Palace looked like, and a vivid idea of the commercial (and artistic) exchanges this exhibition inaugurated.

7f9082fe-da75-56c9-8c44-bba718558f12.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

81c828fc-8155-513b-b95f-cf8966747f0a.description2: In 1865, the United Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia were invited by France to participate in the universal exhibition of 1867, that was to take place in Paris. The Romanian government appointed Alexandru Odobescu to negotiate with the Imperial Commission for the Organization of the Exposition the location of the Romanian pavilion. Although the Principalities were under Ottoman sovereignty, the Commission agreed to offer the Principalities their own pavilion next to that of the Ottoman Empire. Odobescu hired French architect Ambroise Baudry, who had been to Romania in 1864 for an archeological mission, to build the Romanian pavilion, which was a combination of architectural elements characteristic of famous Romanian monuments (e.g.: the Stavropoleos Church in Bucharest, the Curtea de Argeș monastery).

85842d41-d3a1-5921-ac88-903643f0147a.name: Moorish Kiosk in Linderhof Palace Park
85842d41-d3a1-5921-ac88-903643f0147a.type: Pavillion; Park building in Linderhof Palace Park
85842d41-d3a1-5921-ac88-903643f0147a.history:
Linderhof Palace Park was laid out from 1870 to 1880 from plans by Carl von Effner. Ludwig II decorated the park and its environs with architectural features conjuring up the world of the Orient, such as the Moorish Kiosk and the Moroccan House, or scenes from Wagner's operas, such as the Venus Grotto. Hunding's Hut and the Gurnemanz Hermitage.  
The Moorish Kiosk was built in 1867 as the Prussian contribution to the World Exhibition in Paris. In 1870 the "railway king" Henry Strousberg bought the pavilion. After Strousberg's bankruptcy, Ludwig II bought the building in 1876 for Linderhof Palace Park and had it rebuilt and reappointed to his specifications.
85842d41-d3a1-5921-ac88-903643f0147a.keywords: King Ludwig II; Linderhof Palace; Ettal; Moorish style; Romanticism; gardens
85842d41-d3a1-5921-ac88-903643f0147a.description2: The Moorish Kiosk is located high above the park on two terrace levels. A colourful, exotic arrangement of palms, pomegranate trees and numerous flowering shrubs extends the foreign atmosphere of the Kiosk outside the walls and also distinguishes its surroundings from the rest of the park. – Between 1972 and 1983 the kiosk was completely restored.

88ae5c68-848d-500a-a14d-08612e65ec15.name: *Traitor*
88ae5c68-848d-500a-a14d-08612e65ec15.author: Petar Petrovic
88ae5c68-848d-500a-a14d-08612e65ec15.description2: During his frequent travels across the Balkans in the 1880s, Paja Jovanović acquainted himself with the ethnic makeup of the population, particularly in Lower Zeta (present-day Podgorica and the surrounding area), in the neighbourhood of Bar and in the border-lying area with Albania. It was here that Albanian, Serbian and Montenegrin inhabitants intermingled, so their characters, physiognomies, customs and vivid national costumes were entwined and fused into a whole in the paintings of Paja Jovanović. The image of capturing or trying a traitor, who, according to tribal custom, awaited sentencing, is certainly a noteworthy genre subject among those he selected to depict the life and customs of peoples in the Balkans. Unlike the first version, painted by Jovanović in 1885, this replica of The Traitor from the mid-1920s was painted in a more free-handed manner, in broad brush strokes and without insistence on details.

89b9e8c6-f3d0-5b3f-8890-c5a4ed5ba8cf.description2: Vittorio Corcos is well known for his realistic paintings, especially his portraits of women. The woman depicted in the painting *Dreams* is Elena Vecchi, the daughter of a friend of the painter. Elena spent her adolescence at Corcos’ home. Presented in 1897 at the International Exposition Art of Florence, the portrait drew great attention and critical and public acclaim. Given the subject and its allusive title, it’s possible to see the image of a modern, proud and aware young woman that hitherto was represented only in literature: on the contrary, Corcos was able to masterfully represent it in painting. The scene was so admired that it was also reproduced on postcards. Corcos believed that while a portrait of a man has to show his social status, that of a woman always has to be appealing even if she is eighty years old.

8b996198-d4aa-5ddf-8793-9747fc36a20c.name: *1594 Burning of the Remains of St Sava*
8b996198-d4aa-5ddf-8793-9747fc36a20c.author: Petar Petrovic
8b996198-d4aa-5ddf-8793-9747fc36a20c.description2:
The Serb Stevan Aleksić was a student of Nikolaos Gyzis at the Munich Academy of Fine Arts. The painting presented here shows him as a representative of academic realism, yet at the same time testifies to a significant gift for a striking play of light effects.  
In 1594, the Ottoman conquerors burned the remains of the Orthodox Christian saint Sava in Belgrade as a punitive deterrent against Serbian rebellion. St. Sava had played a pivotal role in the early 13th century. He was not just an Orthodox archbishop, but also the author of the first Serbian legal code. The foreign rulers thus asserted an important symbol of their power. In order to preserve the memory of the people's saint, a small church was first built on the site. Then, in 1935, the Serbian Orthodox Church prepared the ground for the St. Sava Cathedral, today one of the largest Orthodox churches in the world.  
It is no surprise that Aleksić made this choice of subject in 1912, considering the political backdrop of the time. It was the year when Serbia joined the Balkan League, which launched the First Balkan War against the Ottoman Empire.

8cbe678a-dcda-57dc-87ce-36a2c9a08898.description2: Paris, International Exhibition, 1878. The text of the magazine describes a big tent built in the garden of the Algerian Pavilion with camel fur, fixed with ropes of the same material and strong bamboo canes. Some Arabian men stayed there, sent by the general Algerian governor, and dressed in the typical light-blue uniform of the "Turkish people", or with a red blanket, typical of the region. The Algerian Pavilion was meant to represent the colony through the reproduction of the Campo Marte and Trocadero buildings and also in the garden.

90b30aa0-1bcb-5a10-80c9-1a254c7529d3.name: A retrospective: Preparations for the exhibition of 1889 - the Eiffel Tower under construction
90b30aa0-1bcb-5a10-80c9-1a254c7529d3.description2: For the Exposition Universelle (world fair) of 1889, France wanted to both celebrate the centenary of the 1789 revolution and also showcase its skill and inventiveness. The Eiffel Tower, a daring move in the world of cast-iron architecture, became first the symbol of the exhibition then of the city as a whole.

9161faa0-4fe2-54c4-a25b-05a4938ccfd9.name: Memorial Volume – Dedicatory and opening ceremonies of the Chicago World's Colombian Exposition – 1893
9161faa0-4fe2-54c4-a25b-05a4938ccfd9.description2: The World's Columbian Exposition or The Chicago World's Fair was a World's Fair held in Chicago in 1893 to celebrate the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus' arrival in the New World in 1492. The fair was an influential social and cultural event to which the Ottoman Empire had been invited. It displayed raw materials and agricultural products at the exposition, as well as handicraft products and plant products belonging to the palace revenue. The 1893 Chicago Exhibition was a big success for the Chamber of Commerce. The Head of the Chamber of Commerce, Azaryan Efendi, was assigned to the head of the commission, which was formed in Istanbul for the Chicago Exhibition.

97c4a755-5c5e-5725-922a-057501cef5ff.name: Medal – The Great Exhibition Palace, London 1851
97c4a755-5c5e-5725-922a-057501cef5ff.description2: This silver medal was dedicated to the palace that was built for the Universal Exposition of London. On the reverse is depicted the Crystal Palace and a short text reads: "Proposed by H.R.H Prince Albert. Designed by Josh Paxton. Erected by Fox Henderson & Co. Occupies 18 acre", while on the obverse is inscribed: "Length 1848 feet. 408 ft. wide. Roof 66 ft. high. Height of transept 108 ft. 900.000 sq. ft. glazed surface. 3320 cast iron columns. 368 wrougth iron trusses. 8 miles exhibition tables. 202 miles of sash bars. 400 tones of glass. Value ₤ 150.000". In 1851, Romanian products (wines, carpets, animal skins, cloths, dyed silk, candles, printings and lithographs, such as a map of the Danubian Principalities) were exhibited in the Turkish pavilion, as Wallachia and Moldavia were under Ottoman sovereignty.

a237773b-cce0-5972-a24d-1e563fd1cb62.description2: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century and as a training school for specialising artisans. The concept was part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The tendency of Murano's industries in using bizarre shapes, often of zoomorphic inspiration, gave life to manufacts not so much functional as extremely representative of the decorative needs, and it was very successful. The motif of glass filaments worked with pincers to look like crests, typical of the 17th century objects, is used also in the little ruby-red jar with gold leaf from the second half of the 19th century and resembling objects from Cinquecento and Seicento.

af2dcc82-957a-54c2-9a0f-e5e5ba86b4d3.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

c16fad3d-de00-51aa-b32f-c08f9761a3dc.keywords: Painting; Halil Pasha; orientalist Turkish painters
c16fad3d-de00-51aa-b32f-c08f9761a3dc.description2: The basis of Turkish painting drawing influence from western tradition was laid when *Mühendishane-i Berr-i Hümayun* (the Naval Academy) opened in 1795. Halil Pasha was foremost among the painters with a military background who founded a western-style art tradition in Turkey. He worked with Jean Leon Gerome in his atelier in Paris. He provided a unique distinction to the analysis of impressionist light and colour, and was an example of artists dealing with impressionist technique. Because of his qualified knowledge about anatomy and his interest in depicting the human figure, Halil Pasha had a unique place in Turkish Art History.

c1c21018-70eb-5e4f-93fb-c53b4de7b9a0.description2: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. The massive emigrations of Murano's glass workers to Spain during the 1600s spurred the building of many kilns that fused formal training with the strong local glass tradition. The *cista* is part of a series of objects made in Murano in the second half of the 19th century, mainly by the Murano Venetian Glass Society, and inspired to Spanish models called "Façon de Venise", showing a Phoenician decoration. The *cista*, or vessel, has a lid with a pinnacle in aquamarine glass.

c25b97af-3b31-51d4-8c86-07d5d3f06ecd.description2: The structure of an Egyptian home was considered particularly interesting and was rebuilt inside the Trocadero Park. The idea and the execution of the house were supported by the famous French Egyptologist Mariette-Bey, who was responsible for numerous excavations along the Valley of Nile and was the founder of the Cairo Museum. This work differs from the one presented by Mariette at the Exhibition in 1867 and was meant to represent a common living building. One room was dedicated to the opening of the Suez Canal and numerous photos and albums provided documentary evidence of Egyptian fashion, oases and travel memories.

c369fdd9-b766-5049-9f4f-a257d2df3d50.description2: Within the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911 and related to the celebrations for the 50th anniversary of the Unification of Italy, a "Forum of Regions" was arranged in the Piazza d’Armi. The architect Ernesto Basile (1857–1932), author of the project for the Sicilian Pavilion, took inspiration from the Arab-Norman architecture in Sicily, in particular from Zisa Palace, the church of Saint John of the Hermits and the Cathedral of Monreale. On the outside, the building looked like a cube with plain walls decorated with blind pointed arches and battlements on top. Doors and windows show pointed arch as well. At the sides of the facades two small towers topped by a small small dome give to the palace a striking oriental look. On the inside, there was an open space with columns topped by capitals, walls decorated with mosaics and majolicas, and fountains.

cbc34421-cbf1-565d-b4bd-d91bdc792930.name: Rosette shaped part of the *minbar* of the Mosque of Ibn Tulun
cbc34421-cbf1-565d-b4bd-d91bdc792930.description:
The mosque of Ibn Tulun was built in Cairo in the 9th century AD, and was restored and renovated during the reign of the Mamluk Sultan Hosam al-Din Lajin in 1296. One of the most important items of the equipment of a mosque is the *minbar* – originally a raised seat – used as a pulpit, but having also a symbolic meaning as the "Throne of Muhammad". The *minbar* was decorated with stone or wood inlays.  
  
The *minbar* of the mosque of Ibn Tulun was one of the most precious. Its wooden decoration was exhibited at the World Trade Exhibition of 1867 in Paris as one of Egypt’s most significant craft works. After that, important pieces of the *minbar* reached numerous European collections.

cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.author: Marina Minozzi
cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.keywords: Italian sculptors; realism; Positivism; Verismo; social topics; post-unitarian Italian society; health; work; rights of workers; peasant; agriculture; working class; social changes; reforms; life expectancy; poverty; literacy; illiteracy; labour

cc3b74af-a7c4-51db-b788-69489a7072e4.description2: In 1880 Achille D’Orsi submitted two artworks, including *Proximus Tuus*, to the National Exhibition of Fine Arts in Brera. The sculpture of *Proximus Tuus* made D’Orsi famous as a member of the Italian “Verismo” school of painting. The misery and harshness of fieldwork is represented for the first time in sculpture to denounce the consequences of the brutalisation of the human beings. This clear social denunciation created the emergence of a huge debate over this issue. The body and the facial expression of the peasant exhausted by labour became a symbol of the working class. The sculpture makes a plea for sympathy and pity for the worker right from the work’s title, expressed in Latin. The subject of the painting has been reproduced and copied several times in order to produce greater awareness over these problems.

ce2e2bbf-52d8-50a7-83d7-5ee68152c911.description2: Rafael Padilla (1868–1917) was born to an African family and sent to Cuba as a slave, where he was bought by a farmer from Bilbao. Once in Paris, he performed as a duo with Footit for twenty years. cf731a2d-eeba-5936-b7db-3a4740cb21ee.keywords: Prints; Entertainment & Leisure; Eating; The Great Exhibition; Menus; Illumination
cf731a2d-eeba-5936-b7db-3a4740cb21ee.description2:
The English architect Owen Jones designed this menu card for a farewell banquet coinciding with the Paris International Exhibition – or Exposition Universelle – of 1867. International exhibitions played an important role in introducing imported styles of ornament. The design of this card echoes illuminated Persian manuscripts, which Jones included in his book Grammar of Ornament.  
Apart from working as an architect, Jones also designed interiors, wallpapers and textiles. He created the interior for the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, which housed the Great Exhibition of 1851.

d07a016a-4cbb-5e3f-8479-fd71b40996a8.name: Exposition in Algiers - façade of the Pavillon des Beaux-Arts, in the Place du Gouvernement
d07a016a-4cbb-5e3f-8479-fd71b40996a8.description2: In 1800, the first "Algerian" exposition was held in Algiers, in a building built especially for this purpose at the Place du Gouvernement (now Place des Martyrs). However, this was in reality an opportunity for France to advertise the "benefits" of colonialism - pacified and economically improved, Algeria was apparently now able to take interest in the arts. The review magazine therefore decided to prioritise paintings with an Algerian theme, irrespective of whether they had been created there or abroad.

d07dfd62-b703-5f69-ae57-1fcc78858569.keywords: Furniture; Exhibition; Art Nouveau; Islamic Art; North Africa; Japan

d07dfd62-b703-5f69-ae57-1fcc78858569.description2:
This chair was made in the workshop of the Italian designer Carlo Bugatti (1856-1940). Bugatti’s furniture attempted to break away from historical conventions, reflecting the Art Nouveau appreciation in nature and the aesthetics of Japan, the architecture of North Africa and the motifs of Islamic art. His use of materials such as painted vellum and stamped brass was also adventurous.  
Bugatti’s designs became very sculptural, using bold geometric forms and large areas of sparsely painted vellum. This chair is similar to one exhibited by Bugatti at the International Exhibition of Modern Decorative Art in Turin in 1902.

d27f7bc1-9e5e-581e-a7d7-9666172ce6a8.name: *The Cock Fight*
d27f7bc1-9e5e-581e-a7d7-9666172ce6a8.author: Petar Petrovic
d27f7bc1-9e5e-581e-a7d7-9666172ce6a8.description2: Among the best known of his Orientalist paintings from the Balkans are those of domestic life, such as *The Cock Fight*. In this painting Jovanović builds a credible, believable scene. The spectators are fully engaged, each one reacts in his or her own particular way, consistent with their age and appearance. The singularity of Jovanović’s approach is even more evident when contrasted to Western European Orientalist paintings such as Jean Léon Gérôme’s famous *The Cock Fight* of 1847 or Ferentz Eisenhut’s depiction of a cock fight in 1894. Awarded the first prize at the Wien Künstlerhaus exhibition 1898, and having a great success at the Paris Salon in 1906, it was widely reproduced in subsequent years and was surely known to Jovanović. It is evident that studies of the figures directly from nature inform this painting. Jovanović was not only providing a new and authentic category of genre paintings but speaking specifically to a culture that was his own. In the process, he was giving significance to an area and ethnic groups heretofore ignored.

d3f8650a-4599-5d0e-a22f-cd44a5f3ea38.name: The Pietroasa Treasure
d3f8650a-4599-5d0e-a22f-cd44a5f3ea38.dates: 4th century AD; discovered in 1837; exhibited in 1867
d3f8650a-4599-5d0e-a22f-cd44a5f3ea38.description2: One of the most valuable gold treasures of Romania is the Pietroasa hoard, which consists of five golden vessels and seven golden pieces of jewelry with a total weight of 19 kg. Dating from the centuries 4-5 AD, the hoard is attributed to the Goths. It was discovered accidentally in April 1837 by two peasants who sold it to an Albanian contractor named Verussi. Knowing that all treasures found in the Romanian soil had to be handed in to the authorities, Verussi tried to hide the hoard and even smashed some of the items to make them smaller. Even though he was eventually caught by the police, from the initial 22 items of the hoard only 12 were recuperated. The Pietroasa treasure was first internationally exhibited in 1867 at the universal exposition in Paris, where it enjoyed a great success.

dfe6e123-1970-5707-8279-08002d40fd1f.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul; Pascal Sebah
dfe6e123-1970-5707-8279-08002d40fd1f.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

e38d66f4-10f9-566e-84d8-1278b05a6847.name: *The Three Ages of Woman*
e38d66f4-10f9-566e-84d8-1278b05a6847.author: Marina Minozzi
e38d66f4-10f9-566e-84d8-1278b05a6847.keywords: International exhibition; universal exposition; art exhibition; Esposizione universale di Roma; Jugendstil;realism; symbol; woman; body; water; gold; glass; metal; mosaic; geometrical motifs; Byzantine; Ravenna; Austrian painters
e38d66f4-10f9-566e-84d8-1278b05a6847.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
e38d66f4-10f9-566e-84d8-1278b05a6847.description2: *The Three Ages of Woman* is one of the few works by Gustav Klimt, the main artist of the Vienna Secession movement, in Italy. The painting was exhibited in 1911 at the International Exhibition of Fine Arts in Rome inside the Austrian Pavilion built by the architect Josef Hoffman (1870-1956). An entire room was dedicated to Klimt (*The Three Ages of Woman*, *The Kiss*, *The Sisters* and several portraits). On this occasion the painting of *The Three Ages of Woman* won a prize and was subsequently bought by the Italian State along with other 51 paintings and seven sculptures in order to be displayed inside the newborn National Gallery of Modern Art in Rome. The canvas, painted in the artist’s maturity, shows an old woman in profile with her body carrying the signs caused by the passing of time. The young woman and mother next to her and frontally depicted, holds her sleeping daughter. The central theme of the canvas is the three steps of woman’s life marked by childhood, maturity and old age. The outstanding “verism”, or “truth” of the figures is in sharp contrast to the decorative background that, with its gold and geometric decorations, is reminiscent of the Byzantine mosaics the artist saw during his voyages to Ravenna in 1903. The use of metals, glaze, coloured glass, and gold show the vogue of orientalism that spread among the artists who wanted to free themselves from western art conventions.

e6f7eabb-fc4e-5c98-b6ca-f2544ae496d9.name: Model in plaster
e6f7eabb-fc4e-5c98-b6ca-f2544ae496d9.description: Following on the European fascination for the oriental world and for the famous Nasrid Palaces of the Alhambra (Granada, Spain), a lot of reproductions of its remarkable architectures and decorations were made and spread. José Contreras was commended as restorer and decorator and his son, Rafael (1824–1890), was the leading pioneer of this trend in 1847. His work was continued by the grandson and by a huge number of plaster-cast workshops in Granada, and very likely, in other cities. His plasterworks were very successful in the International Exhibitions and were kept in private collections and museums like South Kensington (London). This polychrome plaster cast res a window in the Mexnar Palace of Granada (Spain).

e93e2356-ce89-5c16-b735-40f476c4b07d.name: Gustave Eiffel. The Eiffel Tower in 1889.
e93e2356-ce89-5c16-b735-40f476c4b07d.description2: Today, the Eiffel Tower is one of the great symbols of Paris and of France. This metal structure, a huge technological achievement in and of itself, was constructed by Gustave Eiffel (1823–1923) for the Exposition Universelle (world fair) of 1889, which celebrated the centenary of the French revolution. Many of his contemporaries, such as Guy de Maupassant, considered the structure hideous and called for its demolition. This drawing recalls the tower's function as a symbol of the vitality of French industry, highlighting its exceptional size and its proximity to the great Palais de l'Industrie, which housed the Dôme Central, the first building to use electricity on a large-scale.

The new machines changed the printing of journals, achieving up to 18,000 to 20,000 copies per hour. Marinoni had extraordinary success in Paris, where his factory produced 4000 samples of machines which also sold in London, Berlin and Vienna. In Italy at the time, only the journal *Il Secolo* had a "Marinoni".

ecbd97bc-85ed-53b3-ab05-ca13100e4055.description2: Over the centuries the Baths of Diocletian, sacked by the barbarians of Alaric, were abandoned and restored several times. In 1563, Pope Paul IV commissioned Michelangelo to transform it into a church “Santa Maria degli Angeli”. In 1749 the architect Vanvitelli rebuilt it again. For the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, the complex of the "Baths of Diocletian” was restored again under the direction of Rodolfo Lanciani for the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, to host the Archaeological Exhibition dedicated to Roman culture in the Imperial Era with a particular interest for its positive influence on the "ex provinces". The most incredible reconstruction on display was the Temple of Ancyra (ancient capital of Galatia, in the centre of Minor Asia) dedicated to Augustus and the goddess Roma, based on casts taken by the archaeologist Azeglio Berretti. Included in the display are the famous engraved inscription on bronze tablets, the so-called "Res Gestae” that represents the testament of emperor Augustus.

f175d1d2-4ea7-502d-8b4f-2dbcdf510fc9.description2:
Designed by Joseph Nash, this is one of the set of views published with accompanying text as Dickinson's Comprehensive Pictures of the Great Exhibition. The prints used the newly available technique of colour lithography to record scenes from the popular 1851 Exhibition. This particular scene shows the Tunisian exhibit, Tunisia being one of few African countries represented at the Exhibition. Exhibits were selected by the bey, Mushir Basha, and included a Bedouin tent. The wealth of material displayed and the charisma of the exhibitors, Hamda Elmkadden and his assistant Saido Belais, ensured that the exhibit proved ‘one of the most remarkable features’ of the Exhibition.  
Following the Exhibition, a government grant was awarded to a committee headed by Henry Cole to purchase items from the Exhibition to form the basis of a Museum of Manufactures (later the V&A).

f441f874-4d85-5d61-a241-aca16296bfa2.description2: World fairs were an opportunity to discover new inventions, and to make them known worldwide. The "cinematograph" was present, in various forms, at the 1900 Exposition Universelle in Paris. The invention of the "Phono-Cinéma-Théâtre" brought sound and image together for the first time, and Henri Lioret and Clément-Maurice Gratioulet used a phonograph to combine the voices and images of famous actors such as Sarah Bernhardt.

f9bb568b-afa8-55b3-9d37-45f6a17b547a.description2: Fez is an important centre for Moroccan pottery and is particularly associated with a distinctive form of blue and white ceramic ware which became popular in the late 19th century. This dish, or *tabsil*, was used to serve foods with a sauce. The dish was donated to the V&A by George Maw, founder of Maw & Co., a British manufacturer of ceramic tiles. The company won many medals and awards at the international exhibitions which were a feature of the late 19th century. This dish was displayed at the 1871 Annual International Exhibition held in London. A label on its base suggests that it was loaned to the exhibition by George Maw.
